## Discussion

For grouped numeric data, `visstat()` routes test selection from a single
Shapiro--Wilk test on the model residuals. The consequence is intended: normality
tests gain power with sample size and, in large samples, reject departures too
small to affect a mean-based comparison [@Lumley:2002; @Kozak:2018]. Skewed data
are therefore routed to the rank-based branch with probability approaching one as
the number of residuals grows, the switch from mean- to rank-based occurring at
moderate per-group sizes (of order 50 to 100), reproducing and extending earlier
simulations of the pretest-and-route procedure [@Rochon:2012; @Rasch:2011]
([`sw_route_rank_by_skew.R`](sw_route_rank_by_skew.R)). This aligns the test with
the readout: `visstat()` reports these comparisons as box plots, whose median and
interquartile box describe the bulk of the data, while under skew the mean is
drawn toward the long tail and away from that bulk [@Mishra:2019]. Routing skewed
data to a rank-based test --- which compares stochastic ordering rather than
means [@Fagerland:2009] --- therefore matches the comparison to the summary the
figure foregrounds.

That preliminary normality testing invalidates inference [@Franc:2025] holds for
the conditional error of one arm, not for the procedure as a whole, which retains
its nominal level under a common null across skewness 0 to 6
([`sw_gate_typeI_by_distribution.R`](sw_gate_typeI_by_distribution.R);
[@Rochon:2012]). That its size threshold is arbitrary no longer applies: routing
follows residual shape, not sample size.

That Shapiro--Wilk is a normality test rather than a skewness test is correct,
but it is an omnibus statistic whose power is dominated by skewness
[@DAgostino:1973; @Razali:2011] --- a serviceable proxy, and the diagnostic
already on screen. Its rank-routing probability rises with skewness and with the
number of residuals $N$, so that any nonzero skewness is eventually rejected and
larger samples route progressively milder asymmetry to ranks
([`sw_route_rank_by_skew.R`](sw_route_rank_by_skew.R)). The power cost is
negligible --- rank tests retain about 95% efficiency under normality and exceed
the mean-based tests under skew [@Bridge:1999; @Harrell-BBR];
[`sw_gate_power_simulation.R`](sw_gate_power_simulation.R) --- but the hypothesis
tested changes, from equality of means to stochastic ordering, which `visstat()`
reports. At small $N$ the test often fails to detect skewness and keeps the
mean-based route; this affects only group sizes too small for reliable inference.

That one should abandon pre-testing and default to Welch [@Rasch:2011;
@Delacre:2019; @Zimmerman:2004] or to ranks [@Harrell-BBR] fixes the estimand a
priori. The two families answer different
questions: the Wilcoxon--Mann--Whitney null $P(X<Y)=0.5$ coincides with equality
of centres only under a common shape, and under unequal variances can reject when
the centres are equal [@Fagerland:2009]. `visstat()` instead selects between them
and reports the choice.

The mean-based branch is kept because, under normality, its tests are uniformly
most powerful unbiased and alone return an effect and confidence interval on the
data's scale, with the regression and analysis-of-variance structure of the
general linear model [@Bridge:1999; @Harrell-BBR]; the rank branch supplies
robustness under skew. The one intrinsic limitation is that an automated tool
cannot know the research question, and the normality test is a proxy for shape,
not an optimal selection statistic --- for which a shape selector would be more
principled [@Hall:1997] but unreliable at small $N$. `visstat()` therefore
presents the choice as a transparent, overridable default, with its diagnostics
shown.
